title: How a wise person walks
hookLine: how does a person of steady wisdom walk?
carry: steady wisdom: draw in like the tortoise

lines: HOW DOES A WISE PERSON WALK?
cards: How does a wise person walk? It sounds like a riddle, but it's Arjuna's real question near the end of the Gita's second chapter.
Krishna has just described a person whose understanding is steady, and Arjuna wants specifics. How do they speak? How do they sit?
How do they walk? Krishna's answer is the portrait we met three days ago, the one Gandhi kept coming back to. Today we read it slowly, on our last day with Gandhi's Gita.

teach.b: The Sanskrit name for this person is sthitaprajna, one whose wisdom stands firm. In paraphrase: such a person is content in the Self alone.
Sorrow doesn't shake them, pleasure doesn't grab them, and they're free of craving, fear and anger.

teach.h: LIKE A TORTOISE DRAWING IN ITS LIMBS.
teach.b: Then the first image: like a tortoise drawing in its limbs, they can draw the senses back from the things that pull at them. Not destroying the senses. Drawing them in, when needed.
Someone who simply goes without may keep away from what they want, but the taste for it stays behind. Only when the highest is seen does even the taste fall away. Then a stranger picture.
What is night for all beings, the self-controlled one is awake in, and what everyone else is awake to is night for the one who sees. The portrait ends with the sea.

teach.h: RIVERS POUR IN; THE SEA STAYS STILL.
teach.b: Rivers pour into the ocean all the time, and it stays full and unmoved. So is the one into whom desires flow without disturbing them. That one finds peace.
Gandhi held this passage close. On his reading, the battlefield is the heart. Anasakti is how to work on that field without clinging to the fruit.
And the sthitaprajna is what a person looks like after long practice: still walking, still speaking, still in the world, but steady, like the sea.

how: Some Hindus learn the closing verses of the Gita's second chapter, on the person of steady wisdom, by heart and recite them as a daily reading.

o: a Gita that teaches cutting off the senses for good
the Gita as Gandhi read it, aiming at steady wisdom
a Gita about a hermit who leaves the world behind

games.q: the person of steady wisdom — tap the pairs.
p: rivers pour in; it stays still
stays until the highest is seen

s: in the Gita, the person of steady wisdom destroys the senses
the image is a tortoise drawing in its limbs: the senses drawn back when needed, not destroyed.
Krishna says going without is enough to end the taste for things
the taste stays behind, he says, until the highest is seen.
Arjuna's question is about how such a person speaks, sits and walks
he wants the practical marks, and Krishna answers with a portrait.

games.q: you're Arjuna. Krishna has been praising a person of steady wisdom. you want to know what such a person is actually like. what do you ask?
o: what such a person believes about the gods.
how such a person speaks, sits and walks.
where such a person lives, and how to find them.
games.why: Arjuna asks for the marks: how they speak, sit and walk. Krishna's answer is the portrait Gandhi kept close: content in the Self, drawing in like a tortoise, still like the sea.

practice: Notice the senses one at a time, the sounds in the room, the light on your eyelids, the feel of the chair, and draw your attention back from each, the way a tortoise draws in a foot, until what's left is the breath.
If something you want pulls you back out, notice that the taste is still there and let it sit without following it, while you picture the sea staying level as the rivers come in.
If you pray, you can rest in Krishna, or in the one you pray to, as the still water.

wordCard.voice: Gandhi's Gita. The heart as the battlefield, anasakti as the way to work, and the person of steady wisdom, unmoved like the sea, as the goal.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: kurma, tortoise, the image of Gita 2:58 for drawing the senses in.

carryVoice: Your line: steady wisdom, draw in like the tortoise. Tomorrow, a poet and a reed flute. Day nine hundred fifty-nine, done.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 2:54–72 (Arjuna's question; the tortoise, 2:58; the taste that stays, 2:59; night and waking, 2:69; the sea, 2:70)
